Subject: Re: Runway and latency mapping for committed fleet — initial modeling

Olga / Alex — did a quick pass on the token profile. Summary below (raw numbers conservative; based on our A100-80GB baseline with Redwood inference kernel stack and q4_0 quantization). PDF/Excel attached shortly.

Assumptions:
- Model: rwd-4k-q4 (primary) / rwd-8k-q4 (fallback path)
- Median output seq length: 120 tokens; median input ~60 tokens; peak seq length sample up to 2048 in <2% of calls
- Prefix reuse: 30% (chat sessions), reduces decode work for repeated contexts
- Target p95 latency <= 200ms for decode portion (end-to-end measured includes network)
- GPU baseline throughput numbers measured on our internal perf bench (cold KV-cache and warm cache scenarios)

Measured throughput (tokens/sec per GPU, decode-only, single threaded decode path):
- rwd-4k-q4, seq=512 effective: 420 tokens/sec
- rwd-4k-q4, seq=120 effective: 1,050 tokens/sec
- rwd-8k-q4, seq=512 effective: 330 tokens/sec
- rwd-8k-q4, seq=2048 shot: 85 tokens/sec (rare long tails)

Concurrency & SLO fit:
- To keep p95 decode latency <=200ms for median flows (seq ~120) we target per-request decode tokens budget <= 21 tokens/ms -> ~21,000 tokens/sec effective for all concurrent requests on a GPU for the 200ms target. That maps to a practical per-GPU concurrency cap: concurrency = per-GPU-tps / tokens-per-request. With median request ~120 tokens, one GPU at 1,050 tps supports ~8.75 concurrent median requests while staying under the 200ms decode budget in our perf model (includes batching and scheduler overheads).

Burst modeling & headroom:
- Normal sustained demand: 10M tokens / month ≈ 3.86 tokens/sec sustained on average (24/7). But real-time peaks drive the slab sizing. Using the 95th percentile of peak minutes from the token_profile, peak sustained minute-level TPS is ~1,800 tokens/sec.
- For a 2.5x short burst the minute-level peak becomes ~4,500 tokens/sec.

Mapping to reserved GPUs (conservative):
- Baseline (no caching, conservative): assume effective tokens/sec per GPU = 420 (512-like mixed), so to cover 4,500 tps we'd need ~11 GPUs (4500/420 ≈ 10.7) just to keep decode throughput.
- Cache-aware baseline (30% prefix reuse) -> effective demand reduction to ~3,150 tps -> with rwd-4k-q4 seq120 effective at 1,050 tps, we estimate needing 3 GPUs to cover median-style bursts, but because long tails exist we recommend mixing: 4 dedicated GPUs + 2 pre-warmed burst instances (dedicated reserved slots or pre-provisioned hosted) to absorb 2.5x spikes without cross-tenant degradation.

Recommended committed slab (commercial-friendly):
- Committed: 6 GPU-equivalent reserved slots (A100-equivalent) — supports sustained peaks with modest cache and 1.5x margin.
- Burst: 2 pre-warmed reserved burst nodes + hosted overflow policy (auto-fallback to hosted instances when >90% utilization) to cover deeper tails.
- Safety multipliers: 1.5x recommended minimum for business-critical flows, 2.0x if you require near-zero fallback (higher cost).

Latency tradeoffs and fallback:
- For p95 <=200ms with our proposed 6 GPU slab and burst policy, expectation is ~95% of peak minutes served from dedicated capacity; deeper tails offloaded to hosted nodes with slightly higher latency (~300–450ms p95).

I'll attach the Excel with the minute-by-minute simulation and an alternate 2.0x-margin slab. Let me know if you want an aggressive quantization (q2) simulation — that improves token/sec by ~1.6x at some quality-risk tradeoffs.

— Priyom

Recommendation (commercial):
- Commit to a 6-GPU reserved slab (A100-equivalent) on an annual contract. This aligns with the engineering recommendation for 1.5x margin while keeping monthly committed cost within your target.
- Include a 2-node burst reserve (reserved pre-warmed instances billed at lower standby rate) plus an overflow clause to Redwood Hosted to cover rare >2.5x spikes.
- Proposed pricing lever: standard reserved rate for first 6 GPUs, burst nodes at 25% of reserved rate when idle, and usage billing on hosted overflow.

Operational notes:
- We'll provide per-route token/latency dashboards in the Console and a canary/rollback policy for initial 30 days to monitor regressions.
- Contract path: we'll issue a term sheet and a DocuSign package for signature. Included in the package will be a 30-day SLA/monitoring addendum and an option to expand slab mid-term with a 30-day notice.

Deliverables this week:
- Term sheet and draft MSA (legal) for review (Olga to attach).
- Excel cost simulation tied to the two margin scenarios (Priyom's sheet attached).

If that sounds good, Devon — can you confirm your procurement timeline and whether DocuSign is fine? Once we have LOI we can reserve the slab starting the week after signature (subject to region capacity).
